title: Give your Hub deployment a useful structure
description: Connect accounts, sites, groups, cameras and integrations into one understandable setup.

chapters.title: Give each person an appropriate account

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our fictional company has installed Hub for a shop and a warehouse. The owner can sign in. Should every colleague now use that account?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. The configuration guide starts with the owner's broad management role, then describes subaccounts for delegated access. Give people the resources and role they need for their work, rather than passing around the highest-privilege login.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So deciding who can do what is part of configuration, not something to postpone until the end?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. A site operator may need only that site's cameras, with fewer management actions. Check the chosen role and delegated resources together, then verify the result using that person's account.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the difference between making a site and making a group?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A site represents a physical location, such as our warehouse. A group can represent a more abstract collection, such as entrance cameras across locations. That lets the team organise resources around both geography and operational responsibilities.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: A warehouse is a place; entrance cameras are a job-shaped collection. Nice. Does that structure also matter to access?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. The guide uses sites and groups to delegate relevant resources. Build a structure your team can understand, and avoid assuming that an organisational label alone grants every permission.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: We have accounts and tidy location names. Where do the actual camera recordings enter the picture?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Agents need the documented account connection configuration to link their activity to Hub. The Cameras page shows the devices accessible to the current account and offers connection guidance. A site name doesn't establish the upload connection by itself.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we verify before connecting every camera?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Connect one Agent, confirm it appears in the intended account context, and check its recordings and live capabilities. Use the exact instructions for your deployment model and keep account credentials private.

chapters.title: Make integrations serve a clear purpose

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now the warehouse team wants a useful message when a relevant event occurs. How do alerts and channels fit?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An alert describes the event conditions. A channel describes the destination, such as a webhook or another enabled service. Configure both around a clear scenario and verify the whole journey rather than only testing that an endpoint exists.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Start with appropriate accounts, organise sites and groups, connect a real Agent, then test a focused integration. The linked guide supplies the setup details, while the newer topic guides explain individual features and their current limits.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
